mis.m: Thinks 3 + 9 and 9 + 3 must be solved separately and counts all over again for the second one.
mis.why: Students see each fact as a new problem and have not yet noticed that changing the order keeps the total the same.
mis.fix: Build 3 red and 9 blue cubes in a train, then flip the train around and ask, 'Did the number of cubes change?'

mis.m: Adds three numbers left to right only, so 4 + 7 + 6 is done as 11 + 6 instead of spotting 4 + 6 = 10 first.
mis.why: Students believe the order on the page is the order they must add.
mis.fix: Have students circle two addends that make a ten before adding, then add the third number to 10.

mis.m: Uses the turn-around idea for subtraction too, writing 3 − 8 = 5 the same as 8 − 3.
mis.why: Students over-apply the commutative property they just learned for addition.
mis.fix: Act it out with 8 counters and take away 3, then try to take 8 away from 3 counters so students see it does not work.

cra.c: Students build addends with linking cubes or counters in a ten frame, flip or regroup the cubes, and check that the total stays the same. For three addends, they push together the two groups that make 10 first.
cra.r: Students show the same facts on an open number line, jumping 9 then 3 and also 3 then 9, and land on the same number. They draw ten frames to show a make-ten grouping.
cra.a: Students write number sentences such as 3 + 9 = 9 + 3 and 4 + 6 + 7 = 10 + 7, connecting each one to their cubes or jumps.
cra.look: Students turn cube trains around, circle pairs that make ten, and explain why their totals did not change.

assess: Why did you add those two numbers first?
How do you know 5 + 8 and 8 + 5 have the same total?
advance: Can you find a different pair to add first? Is the total the same?
Does the turn-around idea work for 9 − 4? Show me.

assess: Show me how your cube train proves the order does not matter.
Which two numbers made a ten?
advance: Can you write a turn-around fact for 6 + 7?
Which pair would you add first in 2 + 9 + 8? Why?

assess: Count your red cubes. Count your blue cubes.
Is the total the same when you flip the train?
advance: Which two numbers make 10 here?
What is 10 plus 3?
support: Give a two-color cube train and have the student count the total before and after flipping it.
Provide a ten frame so the student can fill one addend and see how many more make ten.

stems: I made a ten with ___ and ___.
d: Apply properties of operations to add and subtract two or three numbers.

mis.m: Sorts only by color or size, putting a big red triangle and a big red square in the same group as 'the same shape.'
mis.why: Color and size are the first things young students notice.
mis.fix: Give shapes all the same color first, then ask, 'How else can we sort these?'

mis.m: Says a long, thin triangle or an upside-down triangle is 'not a triangle.'
mis.why: Students have mostly seen one picture of each shape, sitting flat on its side.
mis.fix: Show many triangles of different sizes and turns, and count the sides and corners together.

mis.m: Cannot name the rule when looking at another student's sort.
mis.why: Students sort by feel without putting the attribute into words.
mis.fix: Have partners guess each other's sorting rule and say it aloud: 'Your rule is shapes with 4 sides.'

cra.c: Students sort pattern blocks, attribute blocks, and paper cutouts of regular and irregular shapes into two or three hoops or trays by a rule such as number of sides or curved and straight sides.
cra.r: Students glue or draw the shapes into a labeled sorting mat or T-chart and write the rule at the top of each column.
cra.a: Students state the rule with informal words, such as 'These have 3 straight sides' or 'These have no corners,' and match it to their sorted groups.
cra.look: Students sort shapes into groups, count sides and corners with their fingers, and tell the rule they used.

assess: What rule did you use to sort?
Why does this shape go in that group?
advance: Can you sort the same shapes a different way?
Where would a shape with 5 sides go?

assess: How many sides does this shape have?
What is the same about all the shapes in this group?
advance: Can you find a shape that would fit in both groups?
What new group would you make for this shape?

assess: Point to a corner. Count the corners.
Is this side straight or curved?
advance: Does this shape belong with these? Why?
Is this still a triangle if I turn it?
support: Start with only two groups and a picture card that shows the rule.
Let the student trace each side with a finger while counting aloud.

stems: This shape goes here because it has ___.
This shape does not belong because ___.
d: Classify and sort regular and irregular two-dimensional shapes based on attributes using informal geometric language.

mis.m: Says a square turned on its corner is 'a diamond, not a square.'
mis.why: Students think the way a shape sits changes what it is.
mis.fix: Turn the same square tile slowly in front of the class and count its 4 equal sides each time.

mis.m: Says a shape is a triangle 'because it is red' or 'because it is small.'
mis.why: Students mix up attributes that describe a shape with attributes that define it.
mis.fix: Keep a T-chart: 'Makes it a triangle' and 'Does not matter,' and sort the words color, size, 3 sides, and 3 corners.

mis.m: Thinks a cube is no longer a cube when it is painted or made larger.
mis.why: Students focus on how the solid looks instead of its faces and edges.
mis.fix: Compare a small wooden cube and a large foam cube and count the square faces on both.

cra.c: Students compare pairs of shapes and solids that differ in color, size, or position but are the same shape, and pairs that look similar but differ in sides or faces.
cra.r: Students draw examples on a two-column chart labeled 'Matters' and 'Does not matter' and add pictures of the same shape in different sizes and turns.
cra.a: Students say the defining rule in a sentence, such as 'A triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners. Color does not matter,' and point to their chart.
cra.look: Students turn, flip, and compare shapes and explain which attributes make the shape what it is.

assess: Why is this still a rectangle?
What makes a triangle a triangle?
advance: If I make it bigger and blue, is it still a square? Why?
What would I have to change to make it not a triangle?

assess: Which column did you put 'color' in? Why?
How many faces does this cube have?
advance: Can you draw a triangle that looks very different from mine?
Is a circle that is tiny still a circle?

assess: Count the sides.
Is it still a square when I turn it?
advance: Does the color change the shape?
Does size change the shape?
support: Use shapes that are all one color so only the number of sides changes.
Give a picture checklist of sides and corners to compare two shapes.

stems: I know it is a ___ because ___.
d: Distinguish between attributes that define a two-dimensional or three-dimensional figure and attributes that do not define the shape.

mis.m: Draws a square with sides that are clearly different lengths and calls it a square.
mis.why: Students know a square has 4 sides but do not yet check that all sides are the same length.
mis.fix: Build squares on a geoboard and count the pegs on each side to check that they match.

mis.m: Leaves a gap at a corner or bends a side when building a triangle, so it is not closed.
mis.why: Students do not yet know shapes must be closed with straight sides.
mis.fix: Use straws or craft sticks so every side is straight, and have students run a finger all the way around to check for gaps.

mis.m: Makes a hexagon with 5 or 7 sides.
mis.why: Students lose track of the sides while building.
mis.fix: Have students put a sticker or mark on each side as they count it.

cra.c: Students build circles, triangles, rectangles, squares, rhombuses, and hexagons with geoboards and bands, straws and connectors, craft sticks, or string.
cra.r: Students draw the same shapes on dot paper or grid paper and label the number of sides and corners.
cra.a: Students name each shape they made and describe it, such as 'My square has 4 sides that are the same length,' tying the words to their drawing.
cra.look: Students build shapes, count and mark the sides, and check that corners touch with no gaps.

assess: How do you know your shape is a square?
How did you make sure your triangle is closed?
advance: Can you make a rectangle that is not a square?
Can you make a different hexagon?

assess: How many sides did you draw?
Are all the sides of your square the same length? Show me.
advance: Can you turn your rectangle into a square?
Can you make a rhombus that is not a square?

assess: Count the sides.
Are there any gaps?
advance: Do you need one more side?
Are these two sides the same length?
support: Provide a picture card of the target shape to copy on the geoboard.
Give the exact number of straws needed for the shape.

stems: I know it is a square because ___.
I can change it to a ___ by ___.
d: Create two-dimensional figures, including circles, triangles, rectangles, and squares, as special rectangles, rhombuses, and hexagons.

mis.m: Says a square is not a rectangle.
mis.why: Students learn 'square' and 'rectangle' as separate names before they see a square as a special rectangle.
mis.fix: Check a square against the rectangle rule together: 4 sides, 4 square corners. 'It passes, so it is a rectangle too.'

mis.m: Calls a rhombus 'a diamond' and does not know its 4 sides are the same length.
mis.why: Everyday language gives students a non-math word for the shape.
mis.fix: Accept 'diamond' as a start, then say the math name and measure the sides with cubes or a paper strip.

mis.m: Counts the same corner twice or skips a vertex when describing a hexagon.
mis.why: Students do not start and end their counting at a marked spot.
mis.fix: Have students put a finger or counter on the first vertex and count around until they get back to it.

cra.c: Students hold and explore pattern blocks, attribute blocks, and tangram pieces, using square corners from an index card to check corners.
cra.r: Students draw and label shapes on dot paper and complete a shape chart with columns for sides and vertices.
cra.a: Students describe shapes using formal words such as sides, vertices, and square corners, for example 'A hexagon has 6 sides and 6 vertices.'
cra.look: Students count sides and vertices, check corners with a card, and use words such as vertex and side out loud.

assess: How do you know this is a rhombus?
Why is a square also a rectangle?
advance: Is every rectangle a square? Show me one that is not.
How is a rhombus like a square? How is it different?

assess: How many vertices does your hexagon have?
Which shapes on your chart have square corners?
advance: Can you draw a shape with 4 sides that is not a rectangle?
What do a triangle and a hexagon have in common?

assess: Point to a vertex.
How many sides does this shape have?
advance: Does it have square corners? Check with the card.
Is this a circle or a hexagon?
support: Give a word card with a picture for side, vertex, and square corner.
Have the student mark each vertex with a counter before counting.

stems: A square is also a rectangle because ___.
These two shapes are alike because ___.
d: Identify two-dimensional shapes, including circles, triangles, rectangles, and squares, as special rectangles, rhombuses, and hexagons and describe their attributes using formal geometric language.

mis.m: Calls a sphere a 'circle' or a cube a 'square.'
mis.why: Students use the flat shape names they know for solid objects.
mis.fix: Trace a face of the cube on paper and say, 'The face is a square. The whole solid is a cube.'

mis.m: Says a cone has 2 faces or does not count the curved surface.
mis.why: Students are unsure how to count curved surfaces and flat faces.
mis.fix: Roll and stack each solid and ask, 'Which part rolls? Which part is flat?'

mis.m: Mixes up a rectangular prism and a triangular prism.
mis.why: Both are prisms and students do not look at the shape of the ends.
mis.fix: Stamp the end faces in paint or trace them and compare the triangle and the rectangle.

cra.c: Students handle geometric solids and real objects such as balls, cans, boxes, party hats, and blocks, and test whether each one rolls, stacks, or slides.
cra.r: Students trace the flat faces of solids on paper and draw or sort pictures of objects into a chart for each solid.
cra.a: Students describe solids using formal words such as faces, edges, and vertices, such as 'A cube has 6 square faces.'
cra.look: Students roll, stack, and trace solids and name each solid and its faces.

assess: How do you know this is a cylinder?
What shape are the faces of this prism?
advance: How is a cube like a rectangular prism?
What real object is shaped like a cone? How do you know?

assess: What did you trace from this solid?
How many faces did you count?
advance: Which solids can roll and stack? Why?
Can you find a solid with a triangle face?

assess: Does it roll?
Point to a flat face.
advance: Is this a sphere or a cylinder?
What shape is this face?
support: Give one solid and one matching real object at a time.
Provide a picture card that shows each solid next to its name.

d: Identify three-dimensional solids, including spheres, cones, cylinders, rectangular prisms (including cubes), and triangular prisms, and describe their attributes using formal geometric language.

mis.m: Places pieces that overlap or leave gaps and says the target shape is done.
mis.why: Students focus on the outline looking close instead of covering it exactly.
mis.fix: Use a puzzle outline mat and ask, 'Can you see any paper peeking through? Is any piece on top of another?'

mis.m: Stops after one way and says there is no other way.
mis.why: Students think a puzzle has only one answer.
mis.fix: Ask, 'Can you make the hexagon with 3 pieces? With 6 pieces?' and post the different ways side by side.

mis.m: Picks pieces at random and gets stuck.
mis.why: Students do not yet plan using sides or corners.
mis.fix: Ask students to match a side of the piece to a side of the outline before placing it.

cra.c: Students use pattern blocks, tangrams, and paper shape cutouts to fill outline mats of a target shape such as a hexagon, rectangle, or large triangle.
cra.r: Students draw or trace their composed shapes on paper or dot paper and color each piece to record each way.
cra.a: Students tell how many pieces and which pieces they used, such as '2 trapezoids make a hexagon' and '6 triangles make a hexagon,' and compare their recordings.
cra.look: Students fill outlines with blocks, find more than one way, and record each way with color.

assess: Which pieces did you use?
How do you know there are no gaps?
advance: Can you make the same shape with more pieces? Fewer?
Which piece could replace these 2 triangles?

assess: How many pieces did you color?
Which way used the most pieces?
advance: Can you find a way nobody has found yet?
How are your two ways alike?

assess: Is the whole shape covered?
Are any pieces on top of each other?
advance: Will this piece fit here? Try turning it.
Can you use 2 triangles here?
support: Give an outline mat with lines showing where each piece goes.
Start with only 2 kinds of pieces to choose from.

d: Compose two-dimensional shapes by joining two, three, or four figures to produce a target shape in more than one way if possible.

mis.m: Cuts a shape into 2 pieces that are clearly different sizes and calls them halves.
mis.why: Students think 'half' means any 2 pieces.
mis.fix: Fold the paper shape and lay one part on top of the other to check if they match.

mis.m: Makes 4 parts by cutting a rectangle into 4 thin strips of different widths.
mis.why: Students count the parts but do not check that they are the same size.
mis.fix: Have students cut out the parts and stack them to compare.

mis.m: Thinks a fourth is bigger than a half because 4 is bigger than 2.
mis.why: Students compare the numbers, not the size of the parts.
mis.fix: Fold one paper square into halves and another into fourths, then hold up one part from each and compare.

cra.c: Students fold and cut paper circles, squares, and rectangles into two and four fair shares, and share play dough or paper 'sandwiches' fairly.
cra.r: Students draw lines on pictures of shapes to show halves and fourths and shade one part.
cra.a: Students describe the parts with words such as 'two halves,' 'four fourths,' 'one half of the circle,' and 'one fourth of the square.'
cra.look: Students fold, cut, and stack parts to check they are equal, and name the parts with words.

assess: How do you know these are fair shares?
What do we call each of the 4 parts?
advance: Can you cut the square into fourths a different way?
Which is bigger, one half or one fourth of the same circle? Why?

assess: How many equal parts did you draw?
Are your parts the same size? How do you know?
advance: Can you show halves with a line going a different way?
If 4 friends share, what do we call each part?

assess: Fold it. Do the parts match?
How many parts are there?
advance: Is this a fair share?
Is each part a half or a fourth?
support: Give paper shapes with a dotted fold line to start.
Use a real share, like a paper cookie for 2 friends, before drawing.

stems: One half is bigger than one fourth because ___.
I cut it a different way by ___.
d: Partition two-dimensional figures into two and four fair shares or equal parts and describe the parts using words.

mis.m: Calls any shape with 2 parts 'halves,' even when the parts are not equal.
mis.why: Students count the parts and do not check the size.
mis.fix: Hold up a non-example and ask, 'If you got this part and I got that part, is it fair?'

mis.m: Says a square cut into 4 triangles from corner to corner is not fourths because the parts are not little squares.
mis.why: Students expect equal parts to look the same as the whole shape.
mis.fix: Cut out the 4 triangles and stack them so students see they match in size.

mis.m: Calls a shape cut into 3 equal parts 'fourths.'
mis.why: Students hear 'fourths' and 'parts' and do not count carefully.
mis.fix: Count the parts aloud together, then ask, 'Is it 2, 4, or something else?'

cra.c: Students sort paper shapes that have been folded or cut into examples and non-examples of halves and fourths, stacking parts to check.
cra.r: Students sort picture cards into 'Halves,' 'Fourths,' and 'Not fair shares' and draw one example and one non-example of each.
cra.a: Students explain each choice with words such as 'This is not halves because the parts are not the same size.'
cra.look: Students sort shape cards, test the parts by folding or stacking, and tell why a card is or is not halves or fourths.

assess: Why is this not an example of fourths?
How did you check that these are halves?
advance: Can you change this non-example into halves?
Can a shape show fourths with parts that look different?

assess: Which pile did you put this card in? Why?
How many parts does this one have?
advance: Draw a non-example of fourths for your partner to fix.
How would you fix this card so it shows halves?

assess: Are the parts the same size?
Count the parts.
advance: Is it halves or fourths?
Would this be fair to share?
support: Give real paper shapes that can be folded instead of picture cards.
Sort only halves and not halves first, then add fourths.

stems: The parts are the same size, so ___.
d: Identify examples and non-examples of halves and fourths.

mis.m: Starts measuring from the end of the tool that is not zero, or from the middle of the object.
mis.why: Students do not know that measuring starts at one end of the object.
mis.fix: Mark a 'start line' with tape and have students line up both the object and the tool there.

mis.m: Counts the marks on a tool instead of the spaces between them.
mis.why: Students count what they see, the lines, instead of the lengths.
mis.fix: Color each space on a paper strip and count the colored spaces, not the lines.

mis.m: Thinks length is only the whole numbers they say, so an object 'between 6 and 7' cannot be measured.
mis.why: Students see length as counting separate things, not as one continuous distance.
mis.fix: Slide a finger along the tool from start to end and say, 'The length keeps going between the numbers.'

cra.c: Students measure classroom objects with simple measuring tools such as linking-cube trains, paper strips marked in equal units, and measuring tapes made of same-size units.
cra.r: Students make their own paper measuring strip by laying same-size units end to end and marking each one, then use it to measure.
cra.a: Students record lengths with a number and a unit, such as 'about 7 cubes long,' and explain where they started and stopped.
cra.look: Students line up objects at a start line, slide fingers along their measuring tool, and record lengths with units.

assess: Where did you start measuring? Why?
What does the number 5 on your strip tell you?
advance: What if the pencil ends between 6 and 7?
Why do we not count the lines?

assess: How did you make your measuring strip?
Show me one unit on your strip.
advance: Does your strip work for a longer object? How?
How is your strip like a cube train?

assess: Put the end here at the start.
Where does it stop?
advance: Count the spaces with me.
Is it longer than 4 units?
support: Tape a start line on the table and a matching start mark on the tool.
Use a strip with each unit in a different color.

d: Use measuring tools to measure the length of objects to reinforce the continuous nature of linear measurement.

mis.m: Leaves gaps or overlaps cubes or paper clips while measuring.
mis.why: Students do not see why the units must touch end to end.
mis.fix: Measure a strip with gaps and then without gaps, and compare the counts together.

mis.m: Mixes long and short units, such as big and small paper clips, in one measurement.
mis.why: Students think any objects in a line count as units.
mis.fix: Ask, 'Are all your units the same size?' and give only one kind of unit.

mis.m: Lays units in a crooked line that goes past or falls short of the object's end.
mis.why: Students do not line units up with the edge of the object.
mis.fix: Have students place the object on a strip of tape and line units along the tape edge.

cra.c: Students lay same-size units such as linking cubes, paper clips, or color tiles end to end along objects with no gaps or overlaps.
cra.r: Students draw the object and the units underneath it, or glue paper units below a picture, showing where the first and last units line up.
cra.a: Students state the length as a number of units, such as 'The book is 9 tiles long,' and explain why the units must touch.
cra.look: Students lay units edge to edge in a straight line and check both ends before counting.

assess: Why do your cubes need to touch?
How do you know you reached the end?
advance: What would happen if there were gaps?
What if one cube was on top of another?

assess: Show me where the first unit starts.
Did your drawing have any gaps?
advance: Can you fix your partner's measurement?
Why do all the units need to be the same?

assess: Are there any gaps?
Is each unit the same size?
advance: Does the last unit reach the end?
Count the units with me.
support: Give a strip of tape to line units along.
Use units that snap together, such as linking cubes.

stems: I lined up the end by ___.
d: Illustrate that the length of an object is the number of same-size units of length that, when laid end-to-end with no gaps or overlaps, reach from one end of the object to the other.

mis.m: Thinks the bigger number always means the object is longer, even with different units.
mis.why: Students compare the counts without thinking about the size of the units.
mis.fix: Measure the same pencil with paper clips and cubes and ask, 'Did the pencil change length?'

mis.m: Expects more big units than small units for the same object.
mis.why: Students have not yet linked a larger unit to fewer units needed.
mis.fix: Measure a table with large and small blocks side by side and compare the two rows.

mis.m: Explains a difference by saying 'I counted wrong' instead of naming the unit size.
mis.why: Students do not yet know different units should give different counts.
mis.fix: Ask, 'Which unit is longer? How does that change the count?'

cra.c: Students measure the same object, like a desk or rug, with two units of different lengths, such as paper clips and linking cubes, or footsteps and hand spans.
cra.r: Students draw two rows of units under the same object picture and label each count.
cra.a: Students compare their counts in words, such as 'It took 6 big clips and 10 cubes because the clips are longer,' and point to their two rows.
cra.look: Students measure with two units, compare the two counts, and tell why they are different.

assess: Why did you get two different numbers?
Did the desk get longer?
advance: If you used an even longer unit, would the number be bigger or smaller?
Why might two friends' footsteps give different counts?

assess: Which row has more units?
Which unit is longer?
advance: Can you guess how many cubes before you measure?
Which unit would you use for the hallway? Why?

assess: Count the clips. Count the cubes.
Which unit is bigger?
advance: Did it take more cubes or more clips?
Did the object change?
support: Measure a short object first with both units side by side.
Give a recording sheet with a picture of each unit.

stems: It is ___ cubes long and ___ clips long.
The object did not change because ___.
d: Measure the same object/distance with units of two different lengths and describe how and why the measurements differ.

mis.m: Gives a number without a unit, such as 'It is 8.'
mis.why: Students do not see the unit as part of the answer.
mis.fix: Ask, '8 what? 8 elephants?' and require a unit word every time.

mis.m: Says the length of an object that ends between 5 and 6 units is 5 every time.
mis.why: Students only count full units they see.
mis.fix: Ask, 'Is the end closer to 5 or to 6?' and point to both.

mis.m: Rounds up because 'it is almost the next one,' even when the end is just past a unit.
mis.why: Students are unsure how to decide 'nearest.'
mis.fix: Use a mark at the middle of a unit and ask which side the end is on.

cra.c: Students measure objects with linking cubes or color tiles and decide which whole unit the end is closest to.
cra.r: Students draw objects next to unit strips and circle the nearest whole unit.
cra.a: Students write and say lengths with a number and a unit, such as 'about 6 cubes,' and explain why they picked that number.
cra.look: Students point to where the object ends, decide which unit is closest, and say the length with a unit.

assess: How did you decide it is about 7 cubes?
What unit did you use?
advance: Is it closer to 4 or 5? How do you know?
Would the answer change with a different unit?

assess: Which number did you circle?
What is the unit?
advance: Why did you not pick the next number?
Can you draw a crayon that is about 3 units long?

assess: Where does it end?
Say the number and the unit.
advance: Is the end closer to this cube or that one?
Is it about 4 or about 5?
support: Use a unit strip with a dot in the middle of each unit.
Give a sentence frame with a space for the unit word.

d: Describe a length to the nearest whole unit using a number and a unit.

mis.m: Reads the minute hand as the hour, so 3:00 is read as 12:00.
mis.why: Students mix up the short hand and the long hand.
mis.fix: Use a clock with the hour hand in one color and say, 'The short hand tells the hour.'

mis.m: Reads half past 4 as 5:30 because the hour hand is close to 5.
mis.why: At half past, the hour hand is between two numbers.
mis.fix: Show the hour hand moving slowly from 4 to 5 and ask, 'Has it reached 5 yet?'

mis.m: Writes 7:3 or 7:03 for seven thirty.
mis.why: Students do not know the minutes part of a digital time uses two digits.
mis.fix: Show a digital clock next to the analog clock and copy the time digit by digit.

cra.c: Students move the hands on geared or student clocks to show times to the hour and half hour, and match them to daily events such as lunch.
cra.r: Students draw hands on clock faces and match analog clock pictures to digital time cards.
cra.a: Students write times in digital form, such as 2:00 and 2:30, and say them as 'two o'clock' and 'half past two.'
cra.look: Students set clocks to times, match analog and digital times, and say the time out loud.

assess: How do you know it is half past 6?
Which hand tells the hour?
advance: Where will the hands be in a half hour?
Why is the hour hand between 6 and 7?

assess: Which card matches this clock?
Show me 9:30 on your clock.
advance: What time comes one hour later?
Can you draw a clock for when you eat lunch?

assess: Point to the short hand.
Where is the long hand?
advance: Is the long hand on 12 or 6?
What number is the short hand on?
support: Use a clock with only the hour hand first.
Color the top half and bottom half of the clock face differently.

stems: The long hand is on ___, so ___.
d: Tell time to the hour and half hour using analog and digital clocks.

mis.m: Makes tally marks without bundling the fifth mark across the first four, then loses count.
mis.why: Students do not yet know the bundle of five.
mis.fix: Model tallies in groups of five and count by fives, then ones.

mis.m: Counts the same object twice or skips one while collecting data.
mis.why: Students do not track which objects they already counted.
mis.fix: Have students move each object into its category pile or cross off each picture as they count it.

mis.m: Makes a fourth category or puts items in the wrong category.
mis.why: Students are unsure of the category rule.
mis.fix: Label each column of the T-chart with a picture and a word before starting.

cra.c: Students sort real objects such as buttons, crayons, or snack shapes into up to three groups and count each group.
cra.r: Students record the counts in a T-chart with tally marks, bundling tallies in groups of five.
cra.a: Students write the number for each category and describe the data, such as 'There are 7 red, 4 blue, and 9 yellow.'
cra.look: Students sort objects, make tally marks, and check their tally counts against the objects.

assess: How did you decide the categories?
How do you know you counted every object?
advance: What if we added a new color? Where would it go?
Which group has the most? How do you know?

assess: Show me your tallies for red.
How many does this bundle of tallies show?
advance: Can you count by fives to check?
How many in all?

assess: Which group does this one go in?
Count the tallies with me.
advance: Is this a group of five?
How many are in this group?
support: Use only two categories at first.
Give a T-chart with picture labels and boxes for tallies.

stems: The group with the most is ___.
d: Collect, sort, and organize data in up to three categories using models/representations such as tally marks or T-charts.

mis.m: Draws pictures of different sizes so a row with fewer pictures looks longer.
mis.why: Students do not know each picture must take up the same space.
mis.fix: Use same-size sticky notes or picture cards to build the graph.

mis.m: Starts bars at different places or forgets to label the categories.
mis.why: Students do not see that a graph needs a starting line and labels.
mis.fix: Draw a bold start line and have students write labels before coloring bars.

mis.m: Colors the bar one box too many or too few.
mis.why: Students count the box lines instead of the boxes.
mis.fix: Have students put a counter in each box first, then color.

cra.c: Students build real graphs with objects or by lining up in rows, and stack linking cubes for each category to make cube towers.
cra.r: Students move their data to picture graphs and bar-type graphs on grid paper, coloring one box for each item and labeling each row or column.
cra.a: Students write a title and labels and match each bar to the number in their T-chart, such as 'The bar for dogs goes to 6.'
cra.look: Students build cube towers, color one box per data point, and add titles and labels to their graphs.

assess: How did you know how tall to make this bar?
Why does each picture need to be the same size?
advance: What would the graph look like if we added 2 more cats?
How is your bar graph like your cube towers?

assess: What is your graph about?
How many does this bar show?
advance: Can you make a picture graph with the same data?
What title would fit your graph?

assess: Color one box for each cube.
Where does the bar start?
advance: How many boxes did you color?
What label goes here?
support: Give a graph with the start line, labels, and title already written.
Build the cube towers first, then lay them on the grid.

d: Use data to create picture and bar-type graphs.

mis.m: Reads the label number next to the bar instead of where the bar ends, or counts the grid lines.
mis.why: Students do not track the top of the bar across to the number.
mis.fix: Lay a strip of paper or a ruler across the top of the bar to the number line.

mis.m: Answers 'how many more' by naming the bigger group's number.
mis.why: Students hear 'more' and pick the larger amount.
mis.fix: Line up the two cube towers side by side and count only the extra cubes.

mis.m: Asks only 'Which has the most?' when making their own questions.
mis.why: Students have seen one type of question many times.
mis.fix: Give question starters such as 'How many more ___ than ___?' and 'How many in all?'

cra.c: Students compare cube towers built from the graph data and match towers to bars.
cra.r: Students read picture graphs and bar-type graphs and mark the top of each bar to answer questions.
cra.a: Students write number sentences such as 8 − 5 = 3 to answer 'how many more' and 4 + 6 + 3 = 13 for 'how many in all,' and write their own questions.
cra.look: Students point to bars, compare them, answer questions, and write their own questions about the graph.

assess: How did you find how many more?
What does this graph tell us?
advance: What question could you ask about this graph?
What would change if 3 friends changed their vote?

assess: How many does this bar show?
Which number sentence matches your answer?
advance: Write a question a friend can answer with this graph.
How many in all? Show me.

assess: Which bar is tallest?
Put your finger on top of the bar. What number?
advance: Which has fewer?
How many more? Count the extra cubes.
support: Give two cube towers to compare before using the graph.
Provide question cards with pictures.

d: Draw conclusions and generate and answer questions using information from picture and bar-type graphs.

mis.m: Thinks any money a person has is income, including money found or given as a gift.
mis.why: Students do not yet connect income to work.
mis.fix: Sort pictures of 'money from doing a job' and 'money from other places.'

mis.m: Thinks money comes from the bank or an ATM, not from work.
mis.why: Students see adults get money from machines.
mis.fix: Tell a short story where a worker earns pay, then puts it in the bank, and then takes it out.

mis.m: Thinks only grown-ups in some jobs earn income.
mis.why: Students know a few jobs well and not others.
mis.fix: Make a class list of jobs, including community helpers and family jobs, that earn income.

cra.c: Students act out simple jobs in a classroom store or community helpers center and receive play coins or bills as pay.
cra.r: Students draw a picture of a person doing a job and earning money and label it 'income.'
cra.a: Students say or write a sentence such as 'Income is money I earn by doing a job,' and point to their picture.
cra.look: Students role-play jobs, get play money for work, and use the word income.

assess: What is income?
How did this worker get income?
advance: Is money from a birthday card income? Why or why not?
What jobs could a kid do to earn income?

assess: Tell me about your picture.
Where did the money come from?
advance: What job would you like to earn income from?
How is income different from a gift?

assess: Did she do a job?
Did she earn money?
advance: Is this income?
What job is this?
support: Use real pictures of workers with the word income.
Act out one job and pay with play coins.

d: Define money earned as income.

mis.m: Says a toy or candy is a need.
mis.why: Students feel strongly about things they want.
mis.fix: Ask, 'Could you live without it?' and sort pictures together.

mis.m: Thinks people can buy everything they want with their income.
mis.why: Students do not yet see that income is limited.
mis.fix: Give a small set of play coins and a picture menu so students must choose.

mis.m: Does not know the difference between goods and services.
mis.why: The words are new to students.
mis.fix: Sort picture cards into 'things you can hold' (goods) and 'jobs someone does for you' (services).

cra.c: Students shop in a classroom store with a limited set of play coins and pictures of goods and services.
cra.r: Students sort picture cards into wants and needs, and into goods and services, on a T-chart.
cra.a: Students explain their choices, such as 'I bought food first because it is a need,' and match words to pictures.
cra.look: Students make shopping choices with limited money and tell whether each item is a want or a need.

assess: Why did you choose that first?
Is this a want or a need?
advance: What would you do if you had less money?
Is a haircut a good or a service?

assess: Which pictures did you put under need?
How did you sort goods and services?
advance: Can you find a want that some people might need?
What did you give up to buy this?

assess: Do you need this to live?
Can you hold it?
advance: Is it a want or a need?
Do you have enough money?
support: Start with only four picture cards.
Give a picture of a family to think about what they need.

d: Identify income as a means of obtaining goods and services, oftentimes making choices between wants and needs.

mis.m: Thinks saving means not having any money at all.
mis.why: Students see money leave when it is spent and do not see saved money as still theirs.
mis.fix: Use a clear jar to collect play coins over several days and count the total.

mis.m: Thinks you can spend money and still save the same money.
mis.why: Students do not see that money used for one choice is gone for the other.
mis.fix: Have students split coins between a 'spend' cup and a 'save' cup and see the coins leave the spend cup.

mis.m: Thinks saving is only for grown-ups.
mis.why: Students have not seen children save for a goal.
mis.fix: Read a story about a child saving for a goal and make a class goal chart.

cra.c: Students split play coins into labeled spend and save jars and use the spend jar in a classroom store.
cra.r: Students draw or color a picture chart showing how much they spent and how much they saved.
cra.a: Students tell the difference, such as 'Spending is using money to buy something now. Saving is keeping money to use later.'
cra.look: Students sort coins into spend and save jars and tell what they will save for.

assess: What is the difference between spending and saving?
Why might someone save?
advance: What could you save for?
What happens if you spend all your money?

assess: Tell me about your chart.
How much did you save?
advance: What could you buy later if you keep saving?
How would your chart change if you spent more?

assess: Is this coin for spending or saving?
Put the save coins in this jar.
advance: Did you spend or save?
Which jar has more?
support: Use two clear jars with picture labels for spend and save.
Start with just a few coins.

d: Distinguish between spending and saving.

mis.m: Thinks charitable giving is only giving money.
mis.why: Students have only heard of giving money.
mis.fix: Make a class list of ways to give, such as time, food, toys, or help.

mis.m: Thinks only rich people can give.
mis.why: Students think giving needs a lot of money.
mis.fix: Share a story of a child who gives a little and how it helps.

mis.m: Confuses giving with trading or paying for something.
mis.why: Students know money moves when we buy.
mis.fix: Ask, 'Did the person get something back?' and sort pictures of giving and buying.

cra.c: Students use play coins and a give jar along with spend and save jars, and take part in a class giving project such as a food or book drive.
cra.r: Students draw a picture of a way to give and add it to a class giving chart.
cra.a: Students say or write how giving helps, such as 'I can give food to help people who need it,' and connect it to their picture.
cra.look: Students share ideas about giving, sort coins into give, spend, and save jars, and talk about who giving helps.

assess: What is charitable giving?
Who could we help?
advance: What are ways to give besides money?
How do you decide how much to give?

assess: Tell me about your giving picture.
Who does your idea help?
advance: What could our class give together?
How does giving make a community better?

assess: Is this giving or buying?
Who gets the help?
advance: Can you give your time?
Which jar is for giving?
support: Use a picture card for give, spend, and save.
Act out giving a toy to a friend.

d: Consider charitable giving.
